title: Design Like a Pro with Canva
tagline: Learn the basics of good design, make your first posts and flyers in Canva, then build a brand, a portfolio and paid design work.
takeaways: Export files ready for print and web
Sell design work with a portfolio
description:
You do not need to be an artist to make designs that look professional. You need a few clear rules and a tool you can use with confidence. This quest teaches both, using Canva as the tool and simple design ideas that work in any app.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **Design basics:** layout, hierarchy, colour, fonts and white space, explained in plain words.
- **Getting around Canva:** the home page and editor in general terms, and how to make any template your own.
- **Your first wins:** a social media post and a simple A4 flyer, from plan to proofread.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **Brand consistency:** brand colours, fonts, logo rules and a brand kit, in general terms.
- **Professional pieces:** presentations, CVs, ads, short videos and correct export and print settings.
- **Portfolio and business:** case studies, packages, clients, scams to avoid, and copyright, licences and image rights.

Canva's menus change over time and some features depend on your plan, so this course teaches ideas you can apply in any version. Follow Ayesha, a student in Lahore, as she turns her uncle's bakery posters around and lands her first paying client.
audience: Students and fresh graduates who want a practical skill for jobs and freelancing
Small-business and home-business owners who make their own posts and flyers
Office staff who prepare presentations, notices and event materials
Job seekers who want a clean CV and confident presentations
Beginners who want to start selling simple design services
outcomes: Apply layout, hierarchy, colour, fonts and white space to make clean, readable designs
Find your way around Canva in general terms and turn any template into your own design

sessions.title: Design Basics: Layout, Hierarchy, Colour, Fonts and White Space
sessions.summary: Learn the five ideas behind every good design: a clear layout, a strong order of importance, a small colour palette, two well-chosen fonts and enough empty space. You will spot what makes a poster messy and fix it with simple rules.
objectives: Explain layout, hierarchy, colour, fonts and white space in plain words
Use size, weight, colour and position to show what matters most
Choose a small colour palette with enough contrast to read easily
Pair two fonts and keep text readable on a phone screen
Use alignment and white space to make a design look calm and professional

cards.title: Too much on one poster
cards.setting: Qureshi Sweets & Bakers, Lahore. A Tuesday evening, two weeks before Eid.

lines.text: Welcome to the Bright Banner quest. Your first stop is a busy bakery in Lahore, where a poster has gone very wrong.
Ayesha beta, I printed fifty of these Eid posters. Six colours, five fonts, every item and price. Nobody reads them. Customers still ask me what the offer is!
Chachu, I can see mithai, rusks, cakes, your phone number, a map and three stars. My eyes do not know where to start.
That is the real problem, Ayesha. A design is not a box to fill. It is a path for the eye. Let us fix it with five simple ideas.
Five ideas? I only want people to know about the Eid gift box.
Then the gift box must be the first thing they see. Everything else supports it. That is called hierarchy, and it is idea number two.

scenes.heading: Layout
scenes.narration: Layout is where things sit on the page. A good layout uses a simple grid, lines things up and groups related items together, so the page feels organised.

scenes.heading: Hierarchy
scenes.narration: Hierarchy is the order of importance. The most important message is biggest or boldest, the next is smaller, and small details come last.

scenes.heading: Colour
scenes.narration: Colour sets the mood and guides the eye. Two or three colours, used on purpose, look stronger than six colours fighting each other.

scenes.heading: Fonts
scenes.narration: Fonts give text its voice. One font for headings and one for body text is usually enough. Readability always comes before decoration.

scenes.heading: White space
scenes.narration: White space is empty space around and between things. It is not wasted. It lets the important parts breathe and makes the design look confident.

cards.title: The hierarchy pyramid
cards.caption: Design from the top down: one main message, a few supporting lines, then the small details.

items.label: Headline
items.detail: The one thing you want people to notice first, such as 'Eid Gift Box'.

items.label: Key detail
items.detail: The offer or the reason to care, such as 'Order by 20 April'.

items.label: Supporting info
items.detail: Short facts like flavours, sizes or a picture of the product.

items.label: Small print
items.detail: Address, phone number, social handle and terms.

cards.question: Bilal's poster has six colours, five fonts and every price at the same size. Which basic idea would help most first?
options: Add a brighter background so the poster stands out more
Use a sixth font for the prices so they look special
Hierarchy: make the Eid gift box the clear main message
Make every item bigger so customers can read all of them
cards.explanation: When everything is the same size, nothing stands out. Choosing one main message and making it the biggest or boldest gives the eye a starting point. Colour and font changes come after the order of importance is clear.

cards.title: Four tools for hierarchy
cards.body:
You can show importance in four simple ways:

- **Size:** bigger things are seen first.
- **Weight:** bold text stands out from regular text.
- **Colour:** a bright or contrasting colour pulls the eye, especially on a calm background.
- **Position:** people usually look at the top and the centre first.

Use one or two of these at a time. If you make the headline big, bold, red and centred, and also make the price big, bold and red, you are back to a crowded page. Pick a winner and let everything else step back.

cards.back: Lining up text and pictures along the same edge or centre line, so the page looks neat and planned.
Putting related things close together, such as a product name and its price, so they read as one group.
A clear difference between things, such as dark text on a light background, so they are easy to see.
Using the same colours, fonts and shapes again, so a design feels like one family.
Invisible rows and columns that help you place things in an orderly way.
The small set of colours you choose for a design and stick to.

cards.title: Serif, sans-serif and display fonts
cards.caption: Choose fonts for their job, not just their looks.

items.label: Look
items.left: Serif fonts have small strokes at the ends of letters
items.right: Sans-serif fonts have clean ends without strokes

items.label: Feeling
items.left: Often feels traditional, formal or elegant
items.right: Often feels modern, simple and friendly

items.label: Good for
items.left: Headings for formal pieces, printed reports and invitations
items.right: Body text on screens, social posts and small labels

items.label: Display or script fonts
items.left: Fancy handwriting styles: fine for one or two words
items.right: Hard to read in long lines or small sizes, so use sparingly

cards.title: The wedding card colours
cards.situation: A neighbour asks Ayesha to make a mehndi invitation. She wants 'all the colours of mehndi': green, yellow, orange, pink, gold and red, all bright, with white text on top. Ayesha tries it and the white text is hard to read on the yellow parts.

choices.text: Pick two main colours plus one accent, and put the text on a calm area with strong contrast.
choices.outcome: The card still feels festive, but now the names and date are easy to read. The neighbour sees the festive feel and can actually read the date.

choices.text: Keep all six colours but add a thin black outline to the text.
choices.outcome: It helps a little, but the card still feels busy and the outline looks rough at small sizes. Better than nothing, not the best fix.

choices.text: Keep the design as it is because the client asked for all the colours.
choices.outcome: Guests struggle to read the date and venue. A designer's job is to guide the client towards something that works, kindly and clearly.

cards.title: Helps or hurts readability?
cards.prompt: Sort each choice by what it does to how easily people can read a design.

items.text: Dark text on a light, plain background
Long paragraphs in a fancy script font
One heading font and one body font
Text placed over a busy photo with no overlay
Generous space between sections
Five different text colours in one line
Text aligned to the same left edge
Tiny text squeezed into the corners

cards.title: Fix a messy design in five steps
cards.caption: Use this order whenever a design feels crowded.

items.label: Choose one message
items.detail: Decide the single most important thing.

items.label: Cut the extras
items.detail: Remove anything that does not support that message.

items.label: Set the hierarchy
items.detail: Make the main message biggest; shrink the rest.

items.label: Align and group
items.detail: Line things up and keep related items together.

items.label: Add breathing room
items.detail: Increase white space around the main message.

cards.question: Ayesha moves the phone number, address and Facebook page next to each other at the bottom of the poster. Which idea is she using?
options: Contrast: making details stand out sharply
Hierarchy: making the details the main message
Repetition: using the same colour in many places
Proximity: grouping related details together
cards.explanation: Contact details belong together. Placing them close to each other tells the reader they are one group of information, and keeps the rest of the poster clear.

cards.title: Before and after: the Eid poster
cards.body:
**Before:** six colours, five fonts, twelve products with prices, a map and three star shapes. Everything shouts.

**After Ayesha's changes:**

- Headline 'Eid Gift Box' at the top in a bold sans-serif, large.
- One clear photo of the box in the middle.
- One line under it: 'Mithai, rusks and dry fruit, ready to gift. Order by 20 April.'
- Phone number and address grouped at the bottom in small, simple text.
- Colours: deep maroon, warm cream and a touch of gold.

The poster now has a lot of empty space. Bilal worried it looked 'too empty', but customers started pointing at the gift box on day one.

cards.title: The squint test
cards.body: Step back from your screen and squint until the design goes blurry. What do you still see? That is what people notice first. If it is not your main message, make the main message bigger, bolder or give it more space, and calm down whatever is shouting instead.

cards.title: Match the problem to the fix
cards.prompt: Match each design problem with the basic idea that fixes it.

pairs.right: Set a hierarchy: make one message the clear winner
Add white space and remove extras
Align them to a shared edge or grid
Increase contrast between text and background
Limit the palette to two or three colours and two fonts

cards.title: Remember from The Blank Page
items: A design is a path for the eye; decide what people should see first.
Show importance with size, weight, colour and position, but pick one clear winner.
Two or three colours and two fonts are usually enough.
Contrast between text and background is the key to readability.
Align and group items so the page looks planned.
White space is not wasted space; it makes designs look confident.

cards.prompt: Find a poster, menu or social media post near you today. Do the squint test. What do you notice first, and is that what the designer wanted? Write one change you would make.

quiz.question: What does 'hierarchy' mean in design?
options: The number of colours used in one design
The way a design is printed and trimmed
The list of fonts that come with a design tool
The order of importance that tells the eye what to see first
quiz.explanation: Hierarchy is the order of importance. It uses size, weight, colour and position to lead the reader from the main message to the details.

quiz.question: Which choice usually makes text easiest to read?
options: Yellow text on a white background
White text on a busy, colourful photo with no overlay
Dark text on a light, plain background
Light grey text on a medium grey background
quiz.explanation: Strong contrast between text and background makes reading easy. Light-on-light or text over busy photos lowers contrast.

quiz.question: How many fonts are usually enough for a simple poster or post?
options: Five, so every line looks different
Two: one for headings and one for body text
One fancy script font for everything
As many as the template offers
quiz.explanation: Two fonts give enough variety for headings and body text while keeping the design calm and consistent.

quiz.question: Ayesha places a product name right next to its price, and far from the shop address. Which principle is she using?
options: Proximity
Repetition
Rotation
Saturation
quiz.explanation: Proximity means placing related items close together so they read as one group, and keeping unrelated items apart.

quiz.question: Bilal says the new poster looks 'too empty'. What is the best reply?
options: You are right, we should fill every corner with more products
Empty space is a printing mistake that should be fixed before printing
We should add a pattern to hide the empty parts
The empty space makes the gift box stand out and look premium
quiz.explanation: White space gives the main message room to breathe. It helps people notice what matters and makes a design look confident.

quiz.question: Which is the best use of a script (handwriting) font?
options: A long paragraph of terms and conditions
Small phone numbers at the bottom of a flyer
One or two words, such as 'Eid Mubarak', at a large size
Every line of a CV so it looks creative
quiz.explanation: Script fonts are decorative and hard to read in long or small text. Use them for a few words at a large size.

quiz.question: What is a design 'palette'?
options: A small set of colours used consistently
A tool for cutting photos into shapes
A list of every colour your screen can show
A folder where you save finished designs
quiz.explanation: A palette is the small group of colours you choose on purpose and stick to, which keeps a design calm and recognisable.

quiz.question: You do the squint test and the first thing you notice is a bright star shape in the corner, not the offer. What should you do?
options: Add another star on the other side for balance
Calm or remove the star and make the offer bigger or bolder
Make the star even brighter so it is clearly the focus
Change every font to bold so the offer can compete
quiz.explanation: The squint test shows what the eye sees first. If it is not the main message, reduce the distraction and strengthen the main message.

quiz.question: Which statement about alignment is correct?
options: Alignment only matters for printed designs, not social posts
Lining items up makes a page look planned
Placing items at random angles always looks more creative
Alignment means using the same colour for every item
quiz.explanation: Alignment creates invisible lines that connect elements. It matters on screens and in print, and it makes designs look organised.

quiz.question: A mehndi card uses six bright colours and the date is hard to read. What is the best fix?
options: Add a seventh colour just for the date
Make the date smaller so it does not clash
Use two main colours and an accent, with the text on a calm area
Keep all six colours and move the date to the back of the card instead
quiz.explanation: A smaller palette with strong contrast keeps the festive feeling while making key information readable.

sessions.title: Getting Around Canva and Editing a Template
sessions.summary: Find your way around Canva's home page and editor, choose a good template and change its text, photos and colours to make it your own. You will learn safe habits like naming, undoing and checking your design before you share it.
objectives: Describe the main parts of Canva's home page and editor in general terms
Choose a template that fits the message, size and audience
Edit text, swap photos, change colours and move or resize elements
Use undo, duplicate, group and layers to work safely
Name, organise and review a design before sharing it

cards.title: Hamza's first click
cards.setting: Ayesha's home in Model Town, Lahore. Her cousin Hamza is visiting from Faisalabad.

lines.text: Ayesha, I need a poster for my university alumni cricket match. I opened Canva and there are thousands of templates. I froze.
I froze too, last week. Sana Apa showed me a trick: search for what you need, then pick the template with the right layout, not the prettiest pictures.
Exactly. Pictures and words are easy to change. A good structure is harder to build. Let us open the editor and look around together.
What if I break something?
You will not. There is always undo, and you can duplicate a design before experimenting. Mistakes in Canva cost nothing but a click.

cards.title: A tour of Canva in general terms

scenes.heading: Home page
scenes.narration: The home page usually has a search bar, suggested design types and your recent designs. Menus and names can move between versions, so look for these ideas rather than exact buttons.

scenes.heading: Search and templates
scenes.narration: Search for a design type, like 'Instagram post' or 'A4 flyer', or for a theme, like 'bakery'. Canva shows templates in that size. Some templates and elements are free; others need a paid plan.

scenes.heading: The side panel
scenes.narration: In the editor, a side panel usually holds templates, elements such as shapes and graphics, text styles, your uploads and more. You drag or click items to add them.

scenes.heading: The toolbar
scenes.narration: Select something on the page and a toolbar shows options for it: font, size, colour, effects, position and transparency. The options change depending on what you selected.

scenes.heading: Share and download
scenes.narration: When you finish, look for the share or download options at the top. You can share a link, invite others to edit, or download a file.

cards.title: Editing a template, step by step
cards.caption: The same simple order works for almost every template.

items.label: Search with purpose
items.detail: Type the design type and topic, such as 'Instagram post cricket'.

items.label: Pick by structure
items.detail: Choose a layout that fits your amount of text and photos.

items.label: Replace the text
items.detail: Click a text box and type your own words.

items.label: Swap the pictures
items.detail: Drag your own photo onto a picture frame or placeholder.

items.label: Adjust colours
items.detail: Change colours to suit your message or brand.

items.label: Check and share
items.detail: Proofread, check on a phone view, then share or download.

cards.question: Hamza finds two cricket templates. One has amazing photos but space for only three words. The other has plain photos and space for a date, venue and team names. Which should he choose?
options: The one with amazing photos, and squeeze his text in later
The one with space for his details, then swap in better photos
Neither, because templates cannot be changed
Both, and put them on top of each other
cards.explanation: Photos are easy to replace. A layout that fits your content is harder to build. Choosing by structure saves time and gives a cleaner result.

cards.back: Undo your last change. Press it again to go further back.
Copy and paste a selected element, like a text box or shape.
Duplicate the selected element in Canva, keeping its style.
Group selected elements so they move and resize together.
Hold Shift and click several elements to select them together.
Before big experiments, make a copy of the whole design so the original stays safe.

cards.title: Elements, frames and layers
cards.body:
Everything you place on a Canva page is an **element**: text boxes, photos, shapes, lines, icons and stickers.

- A **frame** is a shape that holds a photo. Drag a photo onto it and the photo fills the shape, such as a circle for a profile picture.
- **Layers** decide what sits in front and what sits behind. If a text box disappears behind a photo, look for a position or layers option and bring the text forward.
- **Grouping** joins several elements so they move together, such as a logo and its tagline.
- **Locking** stops an element from moving by accident, which is useful for backgrounds.

The exact menu names can change between versions, but these ideas stay the same.

cards.title: The safe editing loop
cards.caption: Work in small steps and check often.

items.label: Change one thing
items.detail: Edit a text box, a photo or a colour.

items.label: Look at the whole
items.detail: Zoom out and check the full design.

items.label: Undo if needed
items.detail: If it looks worse, undo straight away.

items.label: Save a version
items.detail: Copy the design before bigger changes.

cards.title: The disappearing headline
cards.situation: Hamza adds a large photo of a cricket ground to his poster. Suddenly the headline 'Alumni Cup 2026' has vanished. He thinks he has deleted it and starts typing it again in a new text box.

choices.text: Stop, select the photo and send it backward, or bring the headline forward using the layers or position options.
choices.outcome: The original headline appears again, with its font and colour still set. Hamza learns that elements can sit behind each other.

choices.text: Press undo until the photo disappears, then try a smaller photo.
choices.outcome: This works, but he loses the photo he wanted. Knowing about layers would have saved time.

choices.text: Keep typing a new headline on top and ignore the old one.
choices.outcome: Now there are two headlines, one hidden. Later he edits the wrong one and the poster ends up with a typo. Hidden duplicates cause confusion.

cards.title: Swap a photo in a template
cards.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order.
steps: Upload your own photo or pick one from the library
Drag the photo onto the existing picture frame
Double-click the photo to adjust which part shows
Check that the photo does not cover important text
Zoom out and look at the whole design

cards.question: Hamza wants his team logo and its name to stay together whenever he moves them. What should he do?
options: Select both and group them
Lock the background
Duplicate the whole page
Change both to the same colour
cards.explanation: Grouping joins elements so they move and resize as one. Locking keeps a single element fixed in place, which is a different job.

cards.title: Ayesha's template, made her own
cards.body:
Ayesha picks an 'A4 flyer' template for her college's bake sale. It has a large headline, a photo block, three short lines and a footer.

- She changes the headline to 'Bake Sale for the Library Fund'.
- She drags her own photo of brownies onto the photo frame and double-clicks to centre the brownies.
- She changes the template's blue to her college's green using the colour option.
- She deletes one decorative shape that made the footer crowded.
- She renames the file 'Bake sale flyer v1' instead of leaving 'Untitled design'.

In twenty minutes, it looks like her own work, not a copy of a template.

cards.title: Easy to change or hard to change?
cards.prompt: Sort each part of a template by how easily you can change it.

items.text: The words in a text box
A photo in a frame
The colour of a shape
The overall layout and grid
The balance between text and pictures
The number of sections on the page

cards.title: Name and organise from day one
cards.body: Rename every design as soon as you start, such as 'Cricket poster - Alumni Cup - v1'. Keep related designs in a folder. When a client or teacher asks for 'the poster from last month', you will find it in seconds instead of scrolling through fifty untitled designs.

cards.title: Remember from The Template Workshop
items: Search by design type and topic, then choose a template by its structure.
Canva's menus can move between versions; learn the ideas, not exact button positions.
Text, photos and colours are easy to change; layout is the hard part.
Use undo, duplicate, group and layers to work safely.
Some templates and elements are free and some need a paid plan; check before you rely on one.
Name your designs and keep them in folders.

cards.prompt: Open any template you like and change three things: the words, one photo and one colour. What surprised you about how easy or hard each change was?

quiz.question: What is the best way to choose a template?
options: By the prettiest photos, even if the layout does not fit
By the one with the most decorations
By the first one that appears in the search results
By a layout that fits your content
quiz.explanation: Photos and words are easy to replace. A structure that fits your amount of text and images is harder to build yourself.

quiz.question: What does Ctrl + Z (Cmd + Z on a Mac) do in Canva?
options: Undoes your last change
Zooms into the design
Deletes the whole page
Groups selected elements
quiz.explanation: Ctrl + Z is undo on Windows, and Cmd + Z on a Mac. You can press it repeatedly to step back through changes.

quiz.question: A text box seems to have vanished after you added a large photo. What is the most likely reason?
options: Canva automatically deletes any text when a large photo is added
The photo is in front of the text in the layer order
The text was turned into a frame
The design was automatically resized
quiz.explanation: Elements stack in layers. A new photo can sit in front of existing text. Send the photo backward or bring the text forward.

quiz.question: What is a frame in Canva?
options: A shape that holds a photo, which fills the shape
A border you must add to every design
The paid version of a template
A list of your recent designs
quiz.explanation: A frame is a container shape. Drag a photo onto it and the photo fills the shape, such as a circle or a rectangle.

quiz.question: Why should you describe Canva features by idea rather than exact button position?
options: Canva has no buttons, only shortcuts
Buttons are the same on every device forever
Every user sees a completely different product
Menus and names can move between versions
quiz.explanation: Canva updates its interface over time, and some features depend on the plan. Understanding the idea helps you find a feature even after the menu changes.

quiz.question: Which pair of keys groups selected elements in Canva on Windows?
options: Ctrl + Alt + Delete
Ctrl + B
Ctrl + G
Alt + F4
quiz.explanation: Ctrl + G (Cmd + G on Mac) groups selected elements. Ctrl + B usually makes selected text bold, and Alt + F4 closes the window on Windows.

quiz.question: Hamza wants to try a bold new colour scheme but keep his current version safe. What should he do first?
options: Delete the current version and start fresh
Lock every single element on the page so nothing can change by mistake
Make a copy of the design and experiment on the copy
Download it and close Canva
quiz.explanation: A copy protects the original. You can compare both versions and keep the better one.

quiz.question: Which of these is usually the hardest part of a template to change?
options: The overall layout and grid
The words in a text box
The colour of a shape
The photo inside a frame
quiz.explanation: Text, photos and colours change in a click. Rebuilding the layout takes far more work, which is why you choose templates by structure.

quiz.question: A template you like uses a photo marked as needing a paid plan, but you are on a free plan. What is the sensible choice?
options: Screenshot the paid photo and use the screenshot
Ignore the mark because nobody checks
Copy the photo from a search engine instead
Replace it with your own photo or a free one
quiz.explanation: Some elements need a paid plan. Using a screenshot or a random image from the web can break licence terms. Use your own photo or a free element.

quiz.question: Why rename a design from 'Untitled design' straight away?
options: Because untitled designs cannot be downloaded
So you can find it quickly later
Because Canva charges for untitled designs
Because renaming improves the print quality
quiz.explanation: Clear names and folders make your work easy to find, especially when you have many versions or clients.

sessions.title: Your First Wins: A Social Media Post and a Simple Flyer
sessions.summary: Make two real pieces from start to finish: a social media post that stops the scroll and a simple A4 flyer people can read from a distance. You will plan the message, pick the right size, design, proofread and share with confidence.
objectives: Plan a design with a clear goal, audience and single message
Choose a suitable size for a social media post and an A4 flyer
Write short headlines and calls to action that people act on
Make text readable on a phone and from a distance on paper
Proofread and run a final checklist before sharing or printing

cards.title: The new rusk launch
cards.setting: Qureshi Sweets & Bakers, Lahore. Saturday morning, the smell of fresh rusks in the air.

lines.text: Ayesha, we are launching a new atta rusk. I want a post for our page and a flyer for the counter and the mosque notice board.
Two pieces, two jobs. The post must stop people scrolling on their phones. The flyer must be readable from a few steps away.
You already sound like a designer. Before you open Canva, write three things: who it is for, what one thing they should know, and what you want them to do.
For families. New atta rusk, healthy and crunchy. Come and taste it free this weekend.
Then the post says 'New Atta Rusk' big, a crunchy photo, and 'Free tasting this weekend'. Everything else can wait.

scenes.heading: Goal
scenes.narration: What should happen after people see it? Visit the shop, send a message, attend an event or buy online. One goal per design keeps it focused.

scenes.heading: Audience
scenes.narration: Who is it for? Families, students, office staff? The audience shapes your words, photos and colours.

scenes.heading: One message
scenes.narration: Write the main message in a few words, such as 'New Atta Rusk'. If you cannot say it briefly, the design will struggle too.

scenes.heading: Call to action
scenes.narration: Tell people exactly what to do next: 'Taste it free this weekend' or 'WhatsApp us to order'. Make it easy to spot.

scenes.heading: Size and place
scenes.narration: Where will it appear? A square or portrait post for a feed, a vertical story for full-screen phones, or A4 for paper. Check each platform's current recommended sizes.

cards.title: Common starting sizes
cards.caption: Typical sizes many designers start from. Platforms can change their recommendations, so check before you publish.

items.label: Square feed post
items.detail: Works in most social feeds.

items.label: Portrait feed post
items.detail: Takes up more of the phone screen in many feeds.

items.label: Story or reel cover
items.detail: Full-screen vertical; keep text away from the top and bottom edges.

items.label: A4 flyer
items.detail: The standard paper size for flyers in Pakistan and most countries.

cards.question: Bilal wants one design to use as an Instagram story, a square post and a printed A4 flyer without any changes. What should Ayesha explain?
options: Each size needs its own version, laid out for that space
One file works everywhere if the colours are bright
Print shops can stretch any image to A4 without problems
Stories and A4 flyers are the same shape, so it is fine
cards.explanation: Different places have different shapes and viewing distances. Text placed well in a square can be cut off in a story or look tiny on A4. Make a version for each. Canva has a resize feature on some plans, but you should still check and adjust each version.

cards.title: Writing words that work
cards.body:
Design is not only pictures. Short, clear words do most of the work.

- **Headline:** 2 to 6 words, the main message. 'New Atta Rusk' beats 'We are very happy to announce our new product range'.
- **Supporting line:** one short sentence with the benefit. 'Crunchy, wholesome and baked fresh every morning.'
- **Call to action:** a clear next step. 'Free tasting this Saturday and Sunday.'
- **Contact:** only what is needed, such as a WhatsApp number or the shop address.

Read your text out loud. If you run out of breath, it is too long. On social media, many people only read the headline, so make it count.

cards.title: Post or flyer?
cards.prompt: Sort each tip by whether it matters most for a social media post or a printed flyer.

items.text: Must stand out while people scroll quickly on a phone
Must be readable from a few steps away on a notice board
Keep text away from screen edges that apps may cover
Leave a safe margin so the printer does not trim words
Can add a short caption with more detail below it
Shows tear-off strips or an address people can note down

items.label: Viewed on
items.left: A phone screen, usually for a second or two
items.right: Paper on a wall, counter or in a hand

items.label: Text amount
items.left: Very little; details go in the caption
items.right: A little more, but still short and clear

items.label: Headline size
items.left: Large enough to read on a small screen
items.right: Large enough to read from a few steps away

items.label: File type
items.left: PNG or JPG for images, MP4 for video
items.right: PDF for printing, as the printer advises

cards.title: The headline debate
cards.situation: Bilal wants the flyer headline to read: 'Qureshi Sweets & Bakers Proudly Presents Our Brand New Healthy Atta Rusk For Your Family'. It takes up half the flyer and the photo is now tiny.

choices.text: Suggest 'New Atta Rusk' as the headline and move the shop name into a smaller line or logo.
choices.outcome: The headline is now quick to read and the photo has room. Bilal sees that his shop name is still clear, just not shouting. The flyer works from across the room.

choices.text: Keep his headline but make the font smaller so the photo can grow.
choices.outcome: Now the long headline is hard to read from a distance. It is a compromise that weakens both the text and the design.

choices.text: Do exactly what he says without comment.
choices.outcome: The flyer is crowded and the product photo is too small to tempt anyone. Clients pay you for your judgement as well as your hands.

cards.title: Match the part to its job
cards.prompt: Match each part of a design with what it does.

pairs.right: States the main message in a few words
Shows the product and creates appetite or emotion
Gives one key benefit or detail
Tells people exactly what to do next
Shows how to reach or find you

cards.question: Ayesha's square post has the WhatsApp number in small text in the bottom corner. On her phone it is barely readable. What is the best fix?
options: Make the number tiny but bold
Put the number in the caption and keep the post simple
Move it to the very edge so it does not distract
Add three more contact details beside it
cards.explanation: Social posts are seen quickly on small screens. Put details people may want to copy, like a number, in the caption, or make them large enough to read. The image should carry the main message.

cards.title: The finished rusk post and flyer
cards.body:
**The post (1080 x 1350 px, portrait):** a close-up photo of rusks with a cup of chai, headline 'New Atta Rusk' at the top, 'Free tasting this weekend' in a warm button-like shape, and the shop logo small at the bottom. The caption holds the address, timings and WhatsApp number.

**The flyer (A4):** the same photo and colours, headline larger, three short lines, 'Free tasting Saturday and Sunday, 10 am to 8 pm', and the address in clear text with a wide margin from the edges.

They look like a pair because they share the photo, colours and fonts. That repetition helps people recognise the bakery.

cards.title: Final check before sharing
cards.prompt: Put this final checklist in a sensible order.
steps: Read every word slowly, including numbers and dates
Ask someone else to read it once
Check the design on a phone screen or print a test page
Confirm the size and file type are right for where it will go
Download or share, and keep the editable design saved

cards.title: Proofread the numbers twice
cards.body: A spelling mistake is embarrassing. A wrong phone number, date or price costs real money and customers. Read numbers digit by digit, then ask someone else to check them. Bilal once printed 200 flyers with one digit missing from his number, and he still remembers it.

cards.title: Remember from The Launch Wall
items: Before designing, write the goal, the audience, one message and the call to action.
Pick the right size for each place and make a separate version for each.
Keep headlines to a few words and put extra details in the caption.
Flyers must be readable from a distance and keep words away from the trim edges.
Reuse the same photo, colours and fonts so pieces look like a family.
Proofread every number and date twice, and ask a second person.

cards.prompt: Think of a small business or event you know. Write its goal, audience, one message and call to action. Then sketch, on paper, where the headline, photo and call to action would go on a square post.

quiz.question: What should you decide before you open Canva to make a post?
options: The goal, audience, main message and call to action
Which font has the most decorative letters
How many stickers and icons to add
The exact number of colours on the colour wheel
quiz.explanation: Planning the purpose and message first keeps the design focused and saves time on changes later.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest headline for a new product post?
options: We are proud and happy to announce our newest family product
Product update number 4
New Atta Rusk
Click here for more information about things
quiz.explanation: A short headline of a few words is quick to read on a phone and states the main message clearly.

quiz.question: What is a 'call to action'?
options: A phone call from the printer about errors
A clear instruction telling people what to do next
A decorative frame around the headline
The list of colours in a brand palette
quiz.explanation: A call to action, such as 'WhatsApp us to order', turns attention into action.

quiz.question: What is the standard size of A4 paper?
options: 8.5 x 11 inches
quiz.explanation: A4 is 210 x 297 mm. 8.5 x 11 inches is US Letter, 148 x 210 mm is A5 and 297 x 420 mm is A3.

quiz.question: Why should you keep important text away from the top and bottom edges of a story design?
options: Edges always print in a lighter colour
Text at the edges uses more storage space
Canva does not allow text near the edges
Apps often place buttons, names or reply bars there
quiz.explanation: Story screens show profile names, buttons and reply boxes near the edges, which can cover your text.

quiz.question: Where is the best place to put a long address and opening times for a social media post?
options: In tiny text across the whole image
Spread across four corners of the image
In the caption, with the image kept simple
Nowhere, because addresses are never needed
quiz.explanation: The image carries the main message. Details people may want to read or copy fit better in the caption.

quiz.question: Why do the rusk post and flyer share the same photo, colours and fonts?
options: Repetition helps people recognise the bakery across pieces
Canva charges extra for a second photo
Printers can only print one photo per month
Using different fonts on different pieces is not allowed
quiz.explanation: Repeating visual choices builds recognition. People start to link those colours and fonts with the business.

quiz.question: A client insists on a very long headline that crowds the flyer. What is the most professional response?
options: Follow the instruction silently even though it hurts the design
Suggest a short headline and move the rest to a smaller line
Refuse to make the flyer at all
Delete the photo to make room for the words
quiz.explanation: Clients value your judgement. Explaining why a shorter headline works, and showing where the other words can go, keeps both the message and the design strong.

quiz.question: Which mistake on a printed flyer usually causes the most real damage?
options: A wrong digit in the phone number
A slightly different shade of cream in the background
A headline one point bigger than planned
A photo cropped a little tighter than the draft
quiz.explanation: A wrong number means customers cannot reach you, and every printed copy is wasted. Proofread numbers digit by digit.

quiz.question: What is a sensible last step after downloading your finished flyer?
options: Delete the editable design to save space in your Canva account
Rename the file 'Untitled' again
Keep the editable design saved so you can change it later
Change the fonts once more before printing
quiz.explanation: Keeping the editable version lets you fix a date or price later without starting again.

sessions.title: Brand Consistency: Colours, Fonts, Logo Use and a Brand Kit
sessions.summary: Move from one-off designs to a brand that people recognise everywhere. Define brand colours with exact codes, choose brand fonts, set clear rules for logo use and keep them together in a simple brand guide or a brand kit, so every post, flyer and slide looks like it comes from the same business.
objectives: Explain why consistency builds trust and recognition for a business
Define a brand palette with exact colour codes and clear roles for each colour
Choose brand fonts and a text style system for headings, subheadings and body text
Apply logo rules: clear space, minimum size, versions and things never to do
Organise brand assets in a one-page brand guide and, where the plan allows, a brand kit

cards.title: Five bakeries in one feed
cards.setting: Qureshi Sweets & Bakers, Lahore. Three months after the rusk launch, orders are growing.

lines.text: Ayesha, a customer asked if our Facebook page was a different bakery. Look at the last ten posts.
Red here, purple there, a green logo, a blue logo, five different fonts. Even I would not know these are from the same shop.
This is the moment to move from designs to a brand. A brand is the feeling and recognition people have. Consistency is how you build it.
But I like variety. Eid posts should feel different from Ramadan posts.
They can. The theme changes; the brand stays. Same colours, fonts and logo rules, with seasonal photos and accents on top.
So we build a brand vault: the rules and the files, in one place, so anyone who designs for the bakery gets it right.

scenes.heading: Brand colours
scenes.narration: Two to four main colours with exact codes, such as hex codes like #7A1F2B. Each has a role: main colour, background, accent for buttons and highlights.

scenes.heading: Brand fonts
scenes.narration: One heading font and one body font, with set sizes and weights for headings, subheadings and body text.

scenes.heading: Logo and its rules
scenes.narration: The main logo plus versions for light and dark backgrounds, with rules for clear space and minimum size.

scenes.heading: Photo and graphic style
scenes.narration: A consistent look for photos and icons: warm or cool, bright or moody, simple line icons or filled shapes.

scenes.heading: Voice
scenes.narration: How the brand talks: friendly, formal, playful. Words are part of the brand too.

scenes.heading: One home for it all
scenes.narration: A short brand guide document, and on plans that include it, a brand kit inside Canva that stores colours, fonts and logos for quick use.

cards.title: A simple palette with roles
cards.caption: Fictional example palette for the bakery. Exact codes make colours repeatable everywhere.

items.label: Main colour: maroon
items.detail: Headlines, logo and key shapes.

items.label: Background: warm cream
items.detail: Most backgrounds, so designs feel light and warm.

items.label: Accent: gold
items.detail: Buttons, prices and small highlights only.

items.label: Text: dark brown
items.detail: Body text, for strong contrast on cream.

cards.question: Why does the bakery's palette use exact codes like #7A1F2B instead of simply saying 'maroon'?
options: Codes make the colour print brighter than names do
Canva only accepts colour names, never codes
Exact codes are needed to unlock paid templates
Codes make the same colour repeatable on every design
cards.explanation: 'Maroon' can mean many shades. An exact code gives the same colour every time, in Canva and other tools. Colours can still look slightly different on screens and paper, which is why print checks matter.

cards.title: The 60-30-10 idea
cards.body:
A simple way to use a brand palette is the **60-30-10** idea, a guideline rather than a law:

- About **60%** of the design is your calm main or background colour, such as warm cream.
- About **30%** is a secondary colour, such as maroon shapes and headlines.
- About **10%** is the accent, such as a gold button or price tag.

The accent works because it is rare. If gold is everywhere, nothing stands out. Seasonal designs can add a festive accent for a while, but the main brand colours stay in charge.

cards.title: Logo rules every designer should know

cards.back: Keep an empty area around the logo so text and shapes do not crowd it.
Set the smallest size at which the logo stays readable, especially any small text in it.
Have a version for light backgrounds and one for dark backgrounds so it is always visible.
Resize the logo only in proportion. Stretching or squashing makes a brand look careless.
Use only the approved logo colours, not whatever matches today's photo.
Avoid adding shadows, outlines or rotations unless the brand guide allows them.

cards.title: Where is your brand today?
cards.caption: Use this to judge a set of past designs honestly.

items.label: Consistent but dull
items.detail: Same look every time, but nothing stands out or feels fresh.

items.label: Strong brand
items.detail: Recognisable everywhere, with seasonal variety on top of stable rules.

items.label: Invisible
items.detail: Random and plain; people forget the business.

items.label: Eye-catching chaos
items.detail: Each post grabs attention, but nobody links them to one business.

cards.title: The cousin's logo makeover
cards.situation: Bilal's nephew, who is good with phones, has 'improved' the logo for a Ramadan post: stretched it wider, added a glowing outline and changed the maroon to purple to match a photo. Bilal likes it and wants to use it on everything from now on.

choices.text: Thank the nephew, explain the logo rules, and offer a Ramadan design that uses seasonal accents around the unchanged logo.
choices.outcome: Bilal agrees once he sees the seasonal version side by side with the old posts. The logo stays recognisable, and the nephew learns the rules too.

choices.text: Use the new logo only for Ramadan posts, then go back to the original.
choices.outcome: Better than changing it forever, but customers still see two different logos. Seasonal variety belongs around the logo, not in it.

choices.text: Adopt the stretched purple logo on everything because the owner likes it.
choices.outcome: The bakery now has two logos in the world, printed bags no longer match, and the distorted shape looks unprofessional on large prints.

cards.title: On-brand or off-brand?
cards.prompt: Sort each choice for the bakery's designs.

items.text: Cream background with maroon headline and a small gold price tag
Logo stretched to fill the width of a banner
Using the approved heading font for every headline
A new neon green chosen to match one photo
Seasonal crescent graphics around the unchanged logo
Three new fonts added for a 'fun' post
White logo version placed on a dark maroon background

cards.title: Build a brand kit in general terms
cards.caption: On plans that include a brand kit, the idea is the same even if menus move.

items.label: Collect the files
items.detail: Gather the logo versions in good quality, ideally with transparent backgrounds.

items.label: Fix the colours
items.detail: Write down the exact codes and the role of each colour.

items.label: Set the fonts
items.detail: Pick heading and body fonts and decide sizes for each text level.

items.label: Store them together
items.detail: Add colours, fonts and logos to a brand kit if your plan has one, or a shared folder and guide if not.

items.label: Share and review
items.detail: Give the team access and check new designs against the guide.

cards.question: Bilal's Canva plan does not include a brand kit feature. What is a good way to keep the brand consistent anyway?
options: Give up on consistency until he upgrades
Let each person choose their own colours
Keep a one-page brand guide and a master template
Use a different free template every time
cards.explanation: Consistency comes from clear rules, not one feature. A short guide with colour codes, fonts and logo rules, plus a master template with the right styles, works on any plan.

cards.title: Match the brand element to its rule
cards.prompt: Match each element with a sensible rule.

pairs.right: Use sparingly for buttons, prices and highlights
Use for all headlines at agreed sizes
Keep clear space around it and never stretch it
Follow one consistent style, such as warm and bright
Write in the same tone, such as friendly and simple

cards.title: Bilal's one-page brand guide
cards.body:
Ayesha writes a one-page guide that anyone can follow:

| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Colours | Maroon #7A1F2B, Cream #F6EBDD, Gold #C9A227 (accent only), Text #2E1F1A |
| Fonts | One serif for headings, one sans-serif for body; no other fonts |
| Logo | Maroon on light backgrounds, white on dark; clear space equal to the height of the letter Q; never stretched |
| Photos | Natural light, warm tones, real products from the shop |
| Voice | Warm, simple, family-friendly; Urdu and English both fine |

She also makes master templates for a post, a story and an A4 flyer with these styles already set. The shop assistant now makes daily offer posts in five minutes, and they look on-brand.

cards.title: Test your brand in black and white
cards.body: Turn a design to greyscale for a moment, or squint at it. If the logo and headline still stand out, your contrast is good. Also check your colours for people who find some colours hard to tell apart: never use colour alone to show something important, such as 'red means sold out'. Add a word or icon too.

cards.title: Remember from The Brand Vault
items: Consistency builds recognition and trust; themes change but the brand stays.
Define a small palette with exact colour codes and a clear role for each colour.
Use the accent colour sparingly so it keeps its power.
Two brand fonts with set sizes for each text level keep designs consistent.
Respect logo rules: clear space, minimum size, right version, never stretched or recoloured.
Keep everything in a brand guide and master templates, and in a brand kit where your plan includes one.

cards.prompt: Look at the last six posts from a business you like. Which colours, fonts and logo uses repeat? Write a three-line brand guide for that business based only on what you see.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of brand consistency?
options: Designs take longer, so they look more expensive
Every post looks completely new and surprising
The business never needs new photos again
People recognise and trust the business more easily
quiz.explanation: Repeating the same colours, fonts and logo rules helps people recognise a business quickly, which builds trust.

quiz.question: In the 60-30-10 idea, what is the 10% usually used for?
options: The main background colour
An accent for buttons, prices and highlights
Body text across the whole design
The logo's clear space
quiz.explanation: The accent is used sparingly so it stands out and draws attention to key actions or details.

quiz.question: Which of these breaks a common logo rule?
options: Stretching the logo to fill a wide banner
Placing the white logo on a dark background
Keeping empty space around the logo
Resizing the logo in proportion
quiz.explanation: Logos should be resized only in proportion. Stretching distorts the shape and looks unprofessional.

quiz.question: What does 'clear space' around a logo mean?
options: A transparent background behind the logo file
A white box that must always surround the logo
The space between letters inside the logo
An empty area that other text and shapes must not enter
quiz.explanation: Clear space is a protected empty zone around the logo so it is never crowded by other elements.

quiz.question: Why should a brand have both light and dark logo versions?
options: So the logo can change colour every season
Because printers need two logos for every job
So the logo stays visible on any background
So two businesses can share one logo
quiz.explanation: A dark logo on a dark photo disappears. Having approved light and dark versions keeps the logo clear everywhere.

quiz.question: What is the best description of a brand kit in Canva, in general terms?
options: A paid printing service for business cards
A place to store brand colours, fonts and logos for quick use
A set of templates made by other brands
A tool that designs every post for you automatically
quiz.explanation: A brand kit keeps approved colours, fonts and logos together so they are easy to apply. Whether it is available depends on your plan.

quiz.question: Bilal wants Eid posts to feel festive without breaking the brand. What is the best approach?
options: Use a completely new palette and logo for Eid
Keep the brand and add seasonal accents
Change the logo colour to green for the whole month
Use five new festive fonts for the season
quiz.explanation: Seasonal variety sits on top of stable brand rules. The core stays recognisable while the theme feels fresh.

quiz.question: A team member says 'just use maroon'. Why is a hex code like #7A1F2B better?
options: It prints faster on any printer
It makes the colour brighter on screens
It gives the exact shade every time
It is required to download a design
quiz.explanation: Colour names are vague. Exact codes keep colours identical across designs and tools.

quiz.question: Which is the best practice for showing 'sold out' in a menu design?
options: Use a word or icon as well as colour
Use red colour alone with no words
Make sold-out items slightly lighter only
Remove the price and hope people understand
quiz.explanation: Some people find certain colours hard to tell apart. Never rely on colour alone to carry important meaning.

quiz.question: A business has no brand kit feature on its plan. What keeps designs consistent?
options: Choosing new colours for each post
Waiting until the business can upgrade
Asking every designer to guess the fonts
A short brand guide plus master templates
quiz.explanation: Clear written rules and ready-made master templates keep designs on-brand on any plan.

sessions.title: Professional Pieces: Presentations, CVs, Ads, Short Videos and Export Settings
sessions.summary: Design the pieces that win jobs and customers: a clean presentation, a CV that is easy to scan, ads with one clear offer and short animated posts or videos. Then export each one correctly, choosing the right file type, quality and print settings such as bleed and margins.
objectives: Design a clear presentation with one idea per slide and consistent styles
Create a simple, readable CV that people and screening software can follow
Build ads with one offer, one call to action and versions for different sizes
Plan short videos or animated posts that work with the sound off
Choose the right file type and print settings, including resolution, margins and bleed

cards.title: Interview week and a print order
cards.setting: A print shop near Anarkali, Lahore. Hamza is visiting for a job interview; Bilal is ordering 1,000 flyers.

lines.text: My interview at a Faisalabad textile company is on Monday. They want a CV and a five-minute presentation about a marketing idea. My CV is three pages of tiny text.
And the printer says my flyer file is blurry and the edges will be cut off. It looked perfect on my phone!
Two classic problems. Hamza's pieces need to be easy to scan. Bilal's file needs the right export settings for print.
So screens and paper need different settings, and a CV is designed for a busy reader, not to show off.
Exactly. This stage is where good designers become professionals. Same tools, higher standards.

scenes.heading: Presentations
scenes.narration: One idea per slide, a short headline that states the point, large readable text and visuals that support what you say. The slides help the speaker; they do not replace them.

scenes.heading: CV or resume
scenes.narration: Clear sections, a simple layout and plenty of space. Recruiters scan quickly, and many companies use software to read CVs, so keep text as real text in a clear order.

scenes.heading: Ads
scenes.narration: One offer, one call to action and a strong visual. Make versions for each size and placement, and keep claims honest.

scenes.heading: Short videos and animations
scenes.narration: Hook in the first seconds, show the product early, add captions because many people watch with sound off, and keep it short.

scenes.heading: Export and print
scenes.narration: Every piece needs the right file type and settings: PNG or JPG for screens, MP4 for video, PDF for documents and print, with bleed and margins when printing.

cards.title: A CV that works versus a CV that struggles
cards.caption: Simple layouts are easier for both people and screening software.

items.label: Layout
items.left: One or two clear columns with simple headings
items.right: Many boxes, icons and text inside images

items.label: Length
items.left: Usually one to two pages for a fresh graduate
items.right: Three or more pages of every detail

items.label: Text
items.left: Real, selectable text in a readable font
items.right: Skills shown only as star ratings or graphics

items.label: Photo and personal data
items.left: Only what the employer or local custom expects
items.right: Unnecessary details such as ID numbers

items.label: File
items.left: Saved as PDF unless the employer asks for another format
items.right: A screenshot or a phone photo of the CV

cards.question: Hamza found a beautiful CV template where his skills appear as coloured bars, such as 'Excel: 80%'. What is the main problem?
options: Bars say little and may not be read by screening software
Bars make the file too large to email
Coloured bars are not allowed in Pakistan
Bars only work in printed CVs, not PDFs
cards.explanation: A bar showing '80%' tells the employer nothing specific, and graphics may not be read by software that scans CVs. Write skills as text, with evidence: 'Excel: pivot tables and lookup formulas used in a sales report for a student society'.

cards.title: Presentations that help you speak
cards.body:
A good presentation design follows a few habits:

- **One idea per slide.** Split a crowded slide into two.
- **Headline as a sentence** that states the point, such as 'Young buyers discover brands on video first', rather than just 'Research'.
- **Large text.** If people at the back cannot read it, it is too small.
- **Few words.** Key words on screen; the full story in your voice and speaker notes.
- **Consistent styles.** Same fonts, colours and positions on every slide, like a brand.
- **Simple charts.** Highlight the one number that matters and label it clearly.

Canva presentations can include speaker notes, animations and a presenter view in many versions. Use animation lightly: it should guide attention, not distract.

cards.title: Match the export format to its job
cards.prompt: Match each file type with the job it usually suits best.

pairs.right: Sharp graphics, text-heavy images and logos; supports transparent backgrounds
Photos where a smaller file size matters
Flyers, brochures and other printed pieces, with print settings
Videos and animated designs with sound or longer motion
Short, silent looping animations

cards.title: A 15-second animated post
cards.caption: A simple plan for short video or animated posts.

items.label: 0 to 2 seconds: hook
items.detail: A bold visual or question that stops the scroll.

items.label: 2 to 6 seconds: show it
items.detail: The product or offer, clearly, with a short caption.

items.label: 6 to 11 seconds: why it matters
items.detail: One benefit, shown rather than told.

items.label: 11 to 15 seconds: act
items.detail: Call to action and logo, held long enough to read.

cards.title: The blurry, cut-off flyer
cards.situation: Bilal's A4 flyer has a photo running right to the edge and the phone number 2 mm from the bottom. He downloaded it as a small JPG from his phone and sent it on WhatsApp to the printer, who says it will look blurry and the number may be trimmed.

choices.text: Fix the design with a safe margin and bleed, then download a print-quality PDF with bleed and crop marks if the printer wants them, and confirm settings with the printer.
choices.outcome: The printer accepts the file, the photo runs cleanly to the edge, and the phone number is safely inside the margin. Bilal saves money by avoiding a reprint.

choices.text: Download the same design as a high-quality PNG and send it again.
choices.outcome: It may be sharper, but there is still no bleed and the number is still too close to the edge. One problem is fixed; the other remains.

choices.text: Ask the printer to 'just make it work' with the WhatsApp image.
choices.outcome: The printer enlarges the small image, which looks soft, and trims the edge. Bilal pays for 1,000 flyers that look unprofessional.

cards.back: Extra background that runs past the trim line, often about 3 mm, so no white edge appears after cutting. Ask your printer.
Where the paper will be cut to its final size.
An inner zone, kept free of important text, so nothing is cut off if trimming is slightly off.
Small lines outside the design that show the printer where to cut.
How much detail an image holds. About 300 dpi at the final size is a common target for sharp print.
RGB is for screens; CMYK is the ink model many printers use. Colours can shift slightly between them, so ask for a proof.

cards.title: Screen or print?
cards.prompt: Sort each setting by whether it mainly matters for screens or print.

items.text: Bleed and crop marks
Pixel size such as 1080 x 1350

A printed proof to check colours

cards.question: Which design rule matters most for a short video ad in a social feed?
options: Put the logo only at the very end, after 60 seconds
Use long paragraphs of text on every frame
Start with a slow, silent title for ten seconds
Add captions, because many people watch with sound off
cards.explanation: Short feed videos must grab attention quickly and make sense without sound. Captions, an early hook and a clear call to action help.

Set up the design at the final size and keep text inside the safe margin
Use good-quality images that stay sharp at the printed size
Download a print-quality PDF with bleed and crop marks as requested
Check a printed proof before the full print run

cards.title: Hamza's interview pieces
cards.body:
**CV:** one page, two sections side by side only at the top for contact details, then one clear column: profile (two lines), education, two internships with results, a university society project, and skills written as text. Saved as PDF named 'Hamza-Iqbal-CV.pdf'.

**Presentation:** eight slides. Slide headlines are short sentences. One chart highlights a single comparison, labelled clearly. A consistent colour and font on every slide. Speaker notes hold the details he wants to say.

**Result:** the interviewer said the CV was 'easy to read in one minute', and asked Hamza to share the slides with the marketing team. He got a second interview.

cards.title: Honest ads only
cards.body: Ads should make claims you can prove. Do not invent reviews, fake 'before and after' photos or say '50% off' when the price was never higher. Check the advertising rules of each platform before running paid ads, as they change and differ by country. Honest ads protect the client's reputation and yours.

cards.title: Remember from The Print Room

CVs: simple layout, real text, skills with evidence, saved as PDF unless asked otherwise.
Ads: one offer, one call to action, honest claims and a version for each size.
Short videos: hook fast, show the product early, add captions and end with a clear action.
Pick the file type for the job: PNG, JPG, PDF, MP4 or GIF.
For print, use bleed, a safe margin, sharp images and ask the printer for a proof.

cards.prompt: Pick one piece you might need soon: a CV, a presentation or a printed flyer. Write the three most important settings or rules you will check before you share it.

quiz.question: What is 'bleed' in a print design?
options: Ink that spreads when paper is wet
The space between two columns of text
A dark shadow behind the headline
Extra background past the trim line
quiz.explanation: Bleed extends the background beyond where the paper is cut, so small cutting shifts do not leave white edges.

quiz.question: Which file type is usually best for a sharp logo with a transparent background?
options: JPG
PNG
MP4
GIF
quiz.explanation: PNG keeps sharp edges and supports transparency. JPG does not support transparency. In Canva, transparent backgrounds may depend on your plan.

quiz.question: Why should a fresh graduate avoid showing skills only as star ratings or bars?
options: They take too long to print on a home printer
They make the CV more than one page
They give no evidence and may not be read by screening software
Recruiters are not allowed to read graphics
quiz.explanation: Ratings like '4 stars' say nothing concrete. Text with examples is clearer for people and more reliable for software that scans CVs.

quiz.question: What is a good slide headline?
options: A short sentence that states the slide's point
The single word 'Data'
A full paragraph of everything you will say
The company name repeated on every slide
quiz.explanation: A sentence headline tells the audience the takeaway straight away, and the visuals support it.

quiz.question: Why should short social videos include captions?
options: Captions make the file smaller
Many people watch with the sound turned off
Platforms reject videos without captions
Captions replace the need for any visuals
quiz.explanation: Captions let the message work in silence and also help people with hearing difficulties.

quiz.question: What is a common resolution target for sharp printed images at their final size?
options: About 30 dpi
About 72 dpi only
About 300 dpi
About 3,000 dpi
quiz.explanation: Around 300 dpi at the printed size is a common target. Very low resolution looks blurry; much higher adds file size without visible benefit for most print jobs.

quiz.question: What is the 'safe margin' on a flyer?
options: An inner zone kept free of important text so nothing is trimmed
The white border that must surround every flyer
The area where bleed is added outside the trim
A space reserved for the printer's own logo
quiz.explanation: Important text sits inside the safe margin, away from the trim line, so small cutting shifts do not cut it off.

quiz.question: Which file type is usually best for a short, silent looping animation?
options: PDF
JPG
DOCX
GIF
quiz.explanation: GIFs loop short silent animations. MP4 suits longer animations or video with sound.

quiz.question: A client wants an ad saying 'Rated number one bakery in Lahore', but no such rating exists. What should you do?
options: Use the claim because ads always exaggerate
Add a small star so it looks official
Suggest an honest claim instead, such as 'Baked fresh every morning'
Write it in a smaller font so the claim seems less serious to readers
quiz.explanation: Ads must make claims that can be proved. False claims can break platform rules and damage trust. Offer an honest, appealing alternative.

quiz.question: Why are RGB colours on screen sometimes different from the printed result?
options: Printers always make colours brighter on purpose
Screens use light (RGB) while many printers use ink (CMYK)
RGB colours cannot be printed at all
Canva changes colours randomly when downloading
quiz.explanation: Screens mix light; printers mix inks. Some bright screen colours cannot be matched exactly in ink, so a printed proof is wise.

sessions.title: Build a Portfolio, Sell Design Services and Respect Copyright
sessions.summary: Turn your skills into income. Build a portfolio that shows real problems and results, price and package your services sensibly, work with clients professionally and avoid scams. Learn the basics of copyright, licences and image rights, so the work you sell is yours to sell.
objectives: Build a focused portfolio with case studies that show the problem, process and result
Package design services with clear scope, revisions and timelines
Manage clients with briefs, written agreements, advance payments and professional communication
Spot common scams aimed at freelancers and protect yourself
Apply copyright, licences and image rights to templates, fonts, photos, logos and people

cards.title: The first paying client
cards.setting: A video call between Lahore and a boutique in Clifton, Karachi.

lines.text: Ayesha, I saw the bakery's posts and loved them. I run a small clothing boutique in Karachi. Can you design my Eid campaign: posts, stories and a printed lookbook?
Yes! I mean, yes, I would love to. But I have never charged anyone before. How much? How many changes? What if she uses a photo from the internet?
Good questions. Professionals answer them in writing before starting: scope, timeline, revisions, payment and who owns what.
I also need a new logo. Can you make it from one of those Canva graphics?
Careful there. Stock graphics usually come with licence limits, especially for logos and trademarks. Let us learn the rules so you never sell something that is not yours to sell.
Then this is my open studio stage: portfolio, pricing, clients and copyright.

scenes.heading: Portfolio
scenes.narration: A small set of your best work, shown as short case studies: the client's problem, what you did and the result. Quality beats quantity.

scenes.heading: Packages
scenes.narration: Clear service packages, such as 'Social media starter: 8 posts, 2 revision rounds, delivered in 7 days'. Clear scope prevents arguments.

scenes.heading: Clients
scenes.narration: A brief at the start, a written agreement, an advance payment and polite, timely updates. Treat small clients like big ones.

scenes.heading: Safety
scenes.narration: Learn the common scams: fake jobs asking for a fee, overpayment tricks, unpaid 'tests' that are really full projects, and requests to move off a platform.

scenes.heading: Rights
scenes.narration: Know who owns what: your design, the client's logo, stock elements under licence, fonts with their own terms and photos of real people who need consent.

cards.title: Build a portfolio case study
cards.caption: One strong case study beats ten random images.

items.label: The problem
items.detail: What was wrong or needed, in one or two sentences.

items.label: The brief
items.detail: Audience, goal and limits, such as a deadline or brand rules.

items.label: The process
items.detail: Sketches, options and why you chose the final direction.

items.label: The result
items.detail: The final pieces shown as people would see them.

items.label: The impact
items.detail: Honest results or feedback, with the client's permission.

cards.question: Ayesha has no paid clients yet. What is the best way to start a portfolio?
options: Show other designers' work as her own
Wait until she has ten paying clients
Use real small projects and clearly labelled practice briefs
Post unchanged Canva templates as finished work
cards.explanation: Real small projects, like the bakery, and clearly labelled self-set briefs are honest and show skill. Showing others' work or unchanged templates is misleading and can break licence terms.

cards.title: Copyright, licences and image rights in plain words
cards.body:
- **Copyright** protects original creative work, such as photos, illustrations, fonts and designs. Someone owns it, even if it is easy to download.
- **A licence** is permission to use someone's work under certain terms. Canva's free and paid elements come with licence terms; check the current terms for what you may and may not do, such as reselling elements on their own or using them in a trademark.
- **Logos and trademarks:** a logo should be unique. Building it from shared stock graphics may stop the client from owning or registering it. Create original logo shapes instead.
- **Fonts** have licences too. Use fonts that are available in your tool for your use, or that clearly allow commercial use.
- **Image rights:** photos found on search engines are not free to use. Photos of recognisable people, especially children, need their consent.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Rules vary by country, so check the current terms on each platform.

cards.title: Safe to use or check first?

cards.title: The client project cycle
cards.caption: Every project, big or small, follows this loop.

items.label: Brief
items.detail: Ask about the goal, audience, sizes, deadline and brand rules.

items.label: Agreement
items.detail: Confirm scope, revisions, timeline, payment and rights in writing.

items.label: Design
items.detail: Share first drafts, often with a watermark or as low-resolution previews.

items.label: Revise
items.detail: Make agreed changes within the revision rounds.

items.label: Deliver and close
items.detail: Hand over final files after payment, then ask for feedback.

cards.title: The 'test task' message
cards.situation: Ayesha receives a message from a new account: 'We are a big international brand. As a test, design our full Eid campaign: 20 posts and a logo. If we like it, we will hire you for a long project. Also, please pay a small registration fee to join our designer team, and let us talk on WhatsApp instead of this platform.'

choices.text: Decline politely, offer a short paid sample or her portfolio instead, refuse any fee and keep all talks on the platform.
choices.outcome: Ayesha protects her time and money. Real clients look at portfolios or pay for small samples; they do not charge designers to work for them.

choices.text: Do a smaller free test of five posts, but refuse the fee.
choices.outcome: Better than paying, but she may still lose hours of free work to someone who never intended to hire her. A paid sample or portfolio link is safer.

choices.text: Pay the fee and start the 20 posts to make a good impression.
choices.outcome: This has the classic signs of a scam: a fee to join, a huge unpaid 'test' and pressure to leave the platform. She loses money and work.

cards.title: Match the term to its meaning
cards.prompt: Match each business term with what it means.

pairs.right: Exactly what work is included in the price
One agreed set of changes the client can request
Part of the fee paid before work starts
A visible mark on previews so drafts cannot be used without paying
How and where the client may use the final designs

cards.front: Asks you to pay a fee to get work
cards.back: Real clients pay you; they do not charge you to work. Treat this as a scam.

cards.front: Sends too much money and asks for a refund
cards.back: A classic overpayment trick. The first payment often bounces after you refund.
Real tests are short or paid. A full campaign 'test' is free work.

cards.front: Pushes you off the platform at once
cards.back: Moving off a platform can remove its payment protection. Stay on it until you trust the client.
Never share passwords or verification codes with anyone.

cards.question: Zoya asks for 'just a few more changes' after the two agreed revision rounds are used. What is the most professional response?
options: Refuse to reply until she accepts the current design
Agree kindly and quote for the extra round as the agreement says
Make unlimited changes for free to keep her happy
Quietly use her files in other clients' work
cards.explanation: A written agreement lets you handle extra work calmly. Offering an extra round at an agreed rate keeps the relationship friendly and fair.

cards.title: Pricing a design package
cards.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order when setting a price.
steps: List exactly what is included: pieces, sizes and revision rounds
Estimate the hours, including briefing, revisions and file preparation
Look at what similar local designers offer for similar work
Set a package price and the advance you need before starting
Write it in a short proposal the client can accept in writing

cards.title: Ayesha's agreement with Zoya
cards.body:
Ayesha sends a one-page proposal in plain language:

- **Scope:** 10 feed posts, 5 stories and a 12-page lookbook as a print-ready PDF.
- **Logo:** an original logo drawn from scratch, not from stock graphics, with light and dark versions.
- **Timeline:** first drafts in 7 days, finals in 14 days after feedback.
- **Revisions:** two rounds included; extra rounds at a stated rate.
- **Payment:** half in advance, half before final files, using a method both agree on.
- **Rights:** after full payment, Zoya may use the designs for her boutique's marketing; Ayesha may show them in her portfolio after the campaign launches.
- **Photos:** Zoya provides her own product photos and confirms model consent.

Ayesha leaves the actual price for Zoya and herself to agree. Both sign, and the project starts calmly.

cards.title: Price for value, not just hours
cards.body: Do not copy someone else's rates or race to the cheapest price. Consider your hours, your skill, how the client will use the design and the value it creates. A logo used on shop signs and bags for years is worth more than a single post. Raise your prices gradually as your portfolio and reviews grow. Platform fees and rules change, so check the current terms on any freelancing platform you use.
